newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Top German economist Hax says investment too weak.
newsitem.headline: Top German economist Hax says investment too weak.

text.p: Germany's economic recovery remains stable but the low levels of foreign investment due to fiscal uncertainty are dampening hopes of a sustainable upswing, Herbert Hax, chairman of the council of economic advisors known as the "Five Wise Men", said on Friday.
"Investment activity for this phase of the economic cycle remains much too weak," Hax told a briefing in Vienna. Uncertainty over the tax situation in Germany was keeping investors at bay, he noted.

"All indicators point to further cautiousness on the part of the business sector, although the economic situation has clearly improved," he continued, noting investment in Germany was expected to see 3.5 percent growth in 1997.

Investment weakness would continue to hit the job market, Hax noted, projecting for 1997 a rise in unemployment in West Germany to 10.4 percent from 10.1 and a 0.4 percent jobless increase in East Germany to 16.5 percent.

Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) growth was forecast to reach 2.5 percent in 1997, against 1.5 percent in 1996, he said. While exports were seen jumping 6.75 percent, imports remained weak. Production potential, by which the council measures total economic growth, was expected to be meagre in 1997 at just 1.75 percent.

Hax cited "sustainable consolidation of the public budget, reliable prospects for lowering taxes and credible potential for a moderate wage policy" as vital ingredients for breathing new life into the German economy.
"The reliance on budget and currency stability is an important prerequisite for a pick-up in growth," he noted.

Hax reiterated the council's prediction that the budget deficit would be running near 3.3 percent of GDP in 1997, some 12 billion marks off the Maastricht budgetary criteria. -- Vienna newsroom +431 53112 258
